While boosting industrial capacity, weaponizing debt-financed procurement deepens European militarization without direct accountability to Kyiv.

The EU runs a smart selfish maneuver: wrapping domestic defense rearmament in the moral urgency of Ukraine's defense, shifting risk to member states.

Classic Brussels branding—call it a solidarity package, but it's really just a multi-billion euro loan for EU countries to buy weapons.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
EU Pushes Massive New Weapons Buying Spree With Ukraine

‘Ukraine from day one’

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by FOCKE STRANGMANN / AFP via Getty Images)

The European Union is making €21.3 billion, or roughly $23.7 billion, in defense loans available to member states while urging them to purchase weapons alongside Ukraine as Brussels expands its military buildup.

The European Commission opened the second funding round Thursday under its Security Action for Europe (SAFE) initiative, inviting all 27 EU countries to request loans, including those that declined to join its initial round, according to the Commission. Brussels wants participating governments to prioritize air defenses, drones, ammunition and missiles for their own armed forces and Ukraine’s military, the commission said.

The latest allocation is not a new €21.3 billion commitment to Kyiv. It represents unused borrowing capacity within a €150 billion defense loan program adopted in May 2025, after some governments requested less funding than originally anticipated, per the European Commission. (RELATED: NATO Descends Into Circular Firing Squad As Members Fight Over Ukraine Funding)

A decommissioned anti-aircraft tank Flakpanzer Gepard is seen during an exercise of the Panzergrenadier (armoured infantrymen) Training Bataillon 92 during the so-called Spotters’ Day at the military training area in Munster, northern Germany, on June 5, 2026. Along with nine other locations, the Munster site is hosting the Bundeswehr Day open day of the German armed forces on June 6, 2026. (Photo by FOCKE STRANGMANN / AFP)

The loans go to EU member states, which must repay the money, rather than directly to Ukraine. Ukrainian firms can nevertheless supply equipment under eligible procurement projects, according to the EU Council.

The EU finances the program by issuing bonds and providing long-term loans to participating governments. Those governments remain responsible for repayment, per the council.

The Commission is encouraging governments to include cooperative purchases with Ukraine in their defense spending plans, although it has not made Ukrainian participation mandatory, according to its Thursday announcement.

Governments retain responsibility for borrowing while Brussels wants the remaining funds to benefit both their domestic defense industries and Ukraine, European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier explained during a Thursday briefing, according to the European Commission.

“We have obviously associated Ukraine from day one,” Regnier said, adding that the commission was encouraging countries to pursue joint projects as fighting continued, according to the commission briefing.

Nineteen member states joined the original SAFE program, requesting more than €130 billion in financing, according to the European Commission.

The EU has approved loan agreements for all 19 countries, signed agreements with 16 and distributed nearly €13.5 billion in advance payments to 11 governments, per the Commission.

The Commission has not identified which governments will receive money under the new round or how much each will get. It expects to inform applicants of tentative allocations within two weeks after the submission deadline, according to its announcement.

The initiative builds on existing defense cooperation with Kyiv. Fifteen of the 19 national SAFE plans submitted in 2025 already included projects involving Ukraine, according to the EU Council.

Boxer tanks of the German army operate during a presentation at the German army barracks while the German Chancellor (unseen) visits the troops of the German Army in Munster, northern Germany, on April 30, 2026. (Photo by DANIEL REINHARDT / AFP)

SAFE also requires most purchases to involve at least two participating countries, although limited exceptions allow a single member state to buy equipment independently. The goal is to increase production while limiting fragmented weapons purchases across European militaries, according to the EU Council.

The rules also favor European production. No more than 35% of the component costs in eligible weapons systems can generally come from outside the EU, Ukraine or designated European partner countries, according to the council. Eligible purchases reach beyond immediate battlefield needs. The program also covers artillery, ground combat equipment, cybersecurity, naval equipment and electronic warfare capabilities. (RELATED: Zelenskyy’s Former No. 2 Reportedly Hit With Money Laundering Charges)

SAFE is a central component of the EU’s Readiness 2030 initiative, a broader effort to increase military spending and expand European industrial capacity, according to the EU Council.

The second loan round remains an invitation to submit financing requests, not a final weapons order or direct delivery commitment to Ukrainian forces. Proposed projects must still move through the EU’s application and approval process.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Lula Launches Massive Online Censorship Campaign Against 'Electoral Harassment'

Brazil's socialist government announced a series of censorship measures to fight "electoral harassment" in the country's workplaces.
The post Lula Launches Massive Online Censorship Campaign Against ‘Electoral Harassment’ appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
The government of recently reelected socialist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva this week announced a sweeping series of social media censorship measures with the alleged intention of fighting what it called “electoral harassment” in Brazilian workplaces.

The new policies empower Brazilian institutions with the ability to demand the takedown of political content published on social media platforms that is deemed to constitute “harrasment” or “discrimination” against Brazilian workers. The Brazilian Attorney General’s office left open the possibility of potential judicial measures to “fight” said kind of online content.

The measures come just days after Lula was reelected for a fourth term after he defeated conservative Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the October 25 runoff election. According to the Lula administration’s website, government institutions allegedly received numerous complaints from Brazilians who denounced “threats of dismissal and pressure” at their respective workplaces over their political choices. Per the government, the alleged harassment complaints were received as early as Sunday, the day of the election.

“These measures aim to protect workers’ freedom of political choice and hold employers accountable for discriminatory practices,” the Brazilian government said.

The policies are the result of the joint work of a “task force” made up of several Brazilian institutions, including the Labor and Employment Ministry, alongside the Labor Prosecutor’s Office (MPT), the Office of the Attorney General of Brazil, the Superior Labor Court (TST), the Electoral Prosecutor’s Office (MPE), and the Justice Ministry. Among the measures announced by the government are provisions to order the removal of websites, publications, and social media content that the Brazilian government deems to be promoting “persecution or discrimination for political reasons.”

The official website of the Brazilian government, however, does not provide a clear explanation of what types of content would be in violation of the policies. The government, however, specifically mentioned America’s Google and Meta as two examples of the digital corporations that would be subject to takedown notifications under the new framework, based on guidelines from the Brazilian AG’s Office. Lívia Andrade, national attorney for labor and employment, affirmed that the government will also adopt further legal measures against big tech and social media platforms on grounds that complaints of harassment “increased a lot during this post-electoral period.”

Lula had already indicated his intention to carry out more censorship of political voices online through the regulation of social media platforms in his victory speech on Sunday. The Brazilian president affirmed in his speech that his campaign had to overcome external “interference” from social media platforms, stressing, “we have to regulate them.”

“It is not possible for people not to be aware that crime in the digital world needs to be treated as crime in real life,” Lula said.

O Globo detailed on Friday that the Superior Labor Court granted a preliminary injunction from the Labor Prosecutor’s Office against Meta, giving the American tech giant a 24-hour deadline starting on Thursday night to take down posts that encourage “dismissal because of how someone voted.” Additionally, Meta’s platforms, such as Instagram, Facebook, and Threads, must reportedly display “within 72 hours, and for five days” a notice stating that “discrimination based on political beliefs and electoral harassment is prohibited.”

Labor Minister Luiz Marinho stated that a “list” of employers in Brazil found to be involved in “discrimination and electoral harassment” practices will be composed. Entities found in violation of the policies could face the suspension of loans in accordance with local legislation. The Ministry has since opened an official government website to compile complaints from workers who have allegedly been harassed at their workplaces over their political stance.

Similarly, the head of the Superior Labor Court, Justice Vieira de Mello Filho, stated on Thursday that his office will also create a “blacklist” of entities engaged in the alleged politically related harassment of workers, affirming that the consequences for incurring in the yet-to-be explained practices will be “very drastic.”

“The consequences for those who are irresponsibly continuing down this path will be very severe, including restrictions on corporate financing and the possible creation of a blacklist,” Mello Filho said. “This profoundly affects Brazil’s democratic system.”

“Everyone is guaranteed the right to vote freely. No one is obligated to follow anyone else’s instructions,” he continued.

The state-owned news agency Agência Brasil detailed that the government will also carry out an awareness campaign to denounce the described “harassment” practices through Carteira de Trabalho Digital (“Digital Employment Card,”) a work-related smartphone application managed by the Brazilian government.

“The Digital Employment Card will also be used to guide workers on their rights and the procedures for filing complaints. In addition, labor inspectors will be able to identify irregularities, issue infraction notices, and take other appropriate measures,” the Brazilian government said this week.
